Eﬃciency, granulation, and bacterial populations related to pollutant
removal in an upﬂow microaerobic sludge reactor treating wastewater with
low COD/TN ratio
Xiao Zhanga, Bowei Zhaoa, Jia Mengb, Aijuan Zhoua, Xiuping Yuea,⁎, Yukun Niua, Ying Cuia
a College of Environmental Science and Engineering, Taiyuan University of Technology, Taiyuan 030024, PR China
b State Key Laboratory of Urban Water Resource and Environment, Harbin Institute of Technology, 73 Huanghe Road, Harbin 150090, PR China
G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Microaerobic
Nitrogen removal
High-throughput sequencing
Granulation
Ecological mode
A B S T R A C T
In this study, a novel upﬂow microaerobic sludge reactor (UMSR) was constructed to conduct anaerobic di-
gestion of municipal wastewater with low carbon and nitrogen ratio (C/N). Oxygen in the UMSR was supplied by
falling water and external recirculation. Excellent nitrogen removal performance was obtained in the UMSR for
treating wastewater with low C/N ratio at a temperature of 25 °C and a hydraulic retention time of 24 h.
Ammonium and total nitrogen removal eﬃciencies averaged 92.35% and 90.41%, respectively, and sludge
granulation occurred during acclimation. The inferred metabolism of nitrogen removal and ecological positions
of functional microbe were integrated into a granule model by scanning electron microscopy. Additionally, the
analysis of microbial community indicated that aerobic nitrifying bacteria and heterotrophic bacteria survived
on the surface of sludge ﬂoc and granules while the anaerobic autotrophic, heterotrophic denitrifying, and
anaerobic ammonia oxidation bacteria were present in the inner layer.
1. Introduction
Ammonium and organic material in untreated municipal waste-
water are detrimental to the environment of the receiving water (Qin
et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016). Anaerobic digestion process has been
widely investigated for treating municipal wastewater because of its
low sludge and high energy recovery rate (Maharaj and Elefsiniotis,
2001). However, ammonium left in the anaerobic digestion liquid
causes eutrophication (Meng et al., 2015). Therefore, it is necessary to

wastewater. Conventional nitrogen removal is completed through ap-
plication of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), nitrite-oxidizing bac-
teria (NOB), and heterotrophic denitriﬁers in succession (Guo et al.,
2013). The major limitations of conventional nitriﬁcation and deni-
triﬁcation processes include high aeration costs, requirement of addi-
tional carbon sources for denitriﬁcation, and large excess sludge pro-
duction (Kartal et al., 2010a,b; Laureni et al., 2016).
Microaerobic treatment process is an emerging technology for
treating wastewater because of its low dissolved oxygen (DO) demand
with concentrations ranging from 0.3 to 1.0 mg/L (Zitomer, 1998). It is
also characterized by low yield of excess sludge, high chemical oxygen
demand (COD) removal rate, low treatment cost, and small area of
occupation (Zheng and Cui, 2012). Additionally, in the microaerobic
treatment process, organic substances and nutrients can be removed
simultaneously in a single reactor because aerobic bacteria such as
AOB, NOB, and heterotrophic aerobic bacteria can propagate at dif-
ferent depths of biological ﬂocs across DO concentration gradients
(Zheng and Cui, 2012). Microbial populations, including aerobic bac-
teria and facultative aerobic bacteria, can grow on the outer layer of the
activated sludge ﬂoc or granules and consume DO which results in an
anaerobic microenvironment in sludge granules or ﬂoc and allows
anaerobic microorganisms, such as denitrifying bacteria and anaerobic
fermentation bacteria, to live in the inner layer (Liu and Dong, 2011).
Microaerobic biological technology has been proved to remove nitrogen
from domestic wastewater with removal eﬃciencies of around 80%
(Zheng and Cui, 2012). Meng et al., (2018) explored the feasibility of
using microaeration conditions for treating piggery wastewater with a
low C/N ratio, and the total nitrogen (TN) removal in it achieved above
85%.
Filamentous overgrowth in the microaerobic process causes bulking
and loss of sludge. Filamentous bacteria have large speciﬁc surface area
and strong ability to capture low-concentration
organic matter.
Therefore, ﬁlamentous bacteria survive well under the conditions of
low DO and low pollutant concentrations. Granular sludge can eﬀec-
tively relieve sludge bulking and improve settleability of the sludge
(Morgenroth et al., 1997). However, the performance of microaerobic
processes dominated by granular sludge in anaerobic digestion of mu-
nicipal wastewater has received less attention.
In the present study, an upﬂow microaerobic granular sludge re-
actor (UMSR) with falling water and reﬂux was constructed to remove
nitrogen from anaerobic digestion of municipal wastewater with low C/
N ratio. The bubble-free aeration mode in the UMSR reduces the dis-
turbance to granular sludge. The main objectives of this study were to
start-up UMSR, evaluate its pollutant removal performance, and gain a
comprehensive insight into the biological mechanisms and conversions
for simultaneous removal of carbon and nitrogen.
2. Methods
2.1. Experimental set up
The UMSR consisted of a 0.5 m high plexiglass column with an ef-
fective volume of 3.9 L. The bottom of the cylinder was connected to a
0.5 L cone (Fig. 1). The wastewater was fed into the reactor by a peri-
staltic pump. The top of the UMSR was open and the rising water could
overﬂow from the top opening and fall into the reoxygenation water
reﬂux tank around the column. The reoxygenation process was realized
by falling water. A part of the reoxygenated water was reﬂuxed into the
UMSR and the remainder was discharged through the settling tank. The
concentration of DO in the reactor was inﬂuenced by the reﬂux ratio.
2.2. Wastewater and seed sludge
The inﬂuent simulated the municipal wastewater after anaerobic
digestion treatment and was synthetic wastewater of glucose with a
COD concentration of 70 mg/L. The necessary nutrients supplied to
improve sludge growth during the acclimatization of inoculated sludge
are as follows (mg/L): NH4CI (70.0), KH2PO4 (19.7), Na2SO4 (14.2),
MgSO4·H2O (39.0), CaC12·2H2O (36.8), CoC12·6H2O (1.2), NiCl2·6H2O
(1.2), Na2Mo4·2H2O (1.0), FeC13 (5.0), CuSO4·5H2O (5.0), MnSO4·4H2O
(5.0), ZnSO4·7H2O (5.0), and KHCO3 (1200).
The seed sludge for UMSR inoculation was activated sludge ob-
tained from an anoxic tank with ongoing anaerobic/anoxic/oxic (AAO)
process for treating domestic wastewater. The initial biomass in the
UMSR in terms of mixed liquor suspended solids and mixed liquor
volatile suspended solids were 4.66 and 1.29 g/L, respectively.
2.3. Analytical methods
Sampling from the inﬂuent and eﬄuent of the UMSR reactor was
conducted at an interval of two days. All samples were ﬁltered with a
0.45 μm ﬁlter before analysis. TN, NH4
+-N, NO2
−-N, and NO3
−-N were
measured according to standard methods (APHA, 1998). DO, pH, and
temperature were measured by oxygen, pH, and temperature meters
(MT InPro6800, MT FE28, MT Company). Total organic carbon (TOC)
and inorganic carbon (IC) were measured by a TOC analyzer (TOC-V
CPH, Shimadzu Company).
2.4. Operation of the UMSR
First, the DO concentration was adjusted by regulating the reﬂux
ratios at each stage. The DO in the reactor was detected by an on-line
monitoring instrument which was also used to control the aeration of
the reﬂux ratio. The DO values and reﬂux ratios for phases 1, 2, and 3
were 1.53 mg/L, 10:1, 0.37 mg/L, 4:1, and 0.5 mg/L, 5:1, respectively.
The hydraulic retention time (HRT) and temperature in the reactor
were maintained at 24 h and 25 ± 1 °C, respectively.
2.5. DNA extraction and Illumina MiSeq sequencing
The seed sludge, sludge during phase 2 (Day 60), and sludge during
phase 3 (Day 128) were sampled and named S1, S2, and S3, respec-
tively. The total DNA of the samples was extracted using the Bacteria
DNA Isolation Kit Components (MOBIO) according to the manu-
facturer’s instructions. Ampliﬁcations of bacterial 16S rRNA genes for
the V3–V4 regions were performed with bacterial fused primers 341F
and 805R (Herlemann et al., 2011; Hugerth et al., 2014). The speciﬁc
procedure of polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was conducted according
to a previous study (Zhou et al., 2015). The composition of PCR pro-
ducts of V4 region was determined by pyrosequencing using the Illu-
mina Miseq sequencer platform (Shanghai Sangon, China).

2.6. Scanning electron microscopy observation
A sludge sample with a diameter of 0.5 mm was prepared by ﬁxing
the biomass with 2.5% glutaraldehyde with pH 6.8 at 4 °C for 1.5 h. The
sample was washed three times with 0.1 mol/L phosphoric acid buﬀer
at pH 6.8 for 10 min each time. The sample was dehydrated once each
with 50%, 70%, 80%, and 90% ethanol and subsequently thrice with
100% ethanol for 10 min at each instance. Thereafter, the sample was
rinsed for 15 min with a mixed liquor of ethanol and isoamyl acetate in
a volume ratio of 1:1 and pure isoamyl acetate. The sludge sample was
placed in the dryer for seven hours. Subsequently, the sample was
pasted on the scanning electron microscope aluminum plate and
sprayed with gold for one minute.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Pollutant removal eﬃciency of the UMSR
To acclimate the denitrifying bacteria of diﬀerent pathways, the
inoculum was obtained from the anoxic tank in the AAO process be-
cause of the occurrence of denitriﬁcation in the traditional nitrogen
removal process (Chen et al., 2016). According to the pollutant removal
performance of the UMSR, the DO concentration was adjusted step by
step by changing the reﬂux ratio. Additionally, the start-up period was
divided into three phases with aerated water reﬂux ratios of 10:1, 4:1,
and 5:1, respectively.

and the NH4
+-N removal from the reactor eﬄuent on the ﬁrst day was
relatively low. After 30 days (1st–30th days), the eﬄuent NH4
+-N was
reduced to 10 mg/L (Fig. 2) and its removal rate reached 85%. After
acclimation to the high DO in phase 1, the AOB in the seed sludge
recovered activity and proliferated. At the beginning of phase 1, the
concentrations of NO2
−-N and NO3
−-N were very low. However, after
three days, the concentration of NO3
−-N increased sharply to 35 mg/L
at the end of phase 1. A higher reﬂux ratio of 10:1 provided a high DO
of about 1.53 mg/L in the reactor resulting in complete nitration pro-
cess. Because of high DO and low TOC concentrations, the denitriﬁca-
tion capacity of the sludge was insuﬃcient and NO3
−-N could not be
degraded, thus, resulting in high TN concentrations in the eﬄuent.
In phase 2, when the reﬂux ratio was reduced to 4:1, the eﬄuent
NH4
+-N sharply increased to 30 mg/L due to the lack of DO in the ﬁrst
10 days of phase 2. Subsequently, it slowly decreased to 10 mg/L and
reached a steady state on the 100th day. NO2
−-N slowly increased and
then, ﬂuctuated between 7 and 15 mg/L. Nitrite accumulation rate was
found as 42% and the accumulation of nitrite provided a substrate for
anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) and enriched the pathways
of denitriﬁcation (Du et al., 2016). Enrichment of anammox bacteria
(AMX) and autotrophic denitrifying bacteria led to a decrease in NO3
−-
N and an increase in the recovery of TN removal rate from 10% to 80%
at the beginning of phase 2. In the latter part of phase 2, nitrate gra-
dually decreased to 2 mg/L.
In phase 3, the increase of the reﬂux ratio allowed the AOB to utilise
more DO, resulting in a further decrease in NH4
+-N and a slight in-
crease in NO3
−-N to 5 mg/L in the eﬄuent. Finally, NH4
+-N was re-
duced to less than 3 mg/L and the removal rate was above 95%. NO2
−-
N and NO3
−-N were less than 1 and 5 mg/L, respectively. The total
nitrogen removal rate was more than 90% and excellent nitrogen re-
moval performance was obtained in the UMSR at 25 °C at an HRT of
24 h.
The removal rates of TOC and IC are closely related to the nitrogen
removal performance. The removal rate of IC increased from 30% in
phase 1 to 67% at the end of phase 3. As the removal rate of NH4
+-N
increased, the removal rate of IC correspondingly increased. The IC is
used by autotrophic bacteria (AOB, NOB, and AMX) for growth and
biosynthesis. The removal rate of TOC remained almost unchanged
during the whole acclimation process.
The pH of the inﬂuent was higher than that of the eﬄuent at the
initial phase of start-up. With the extension of acclimation time and
improvement of the denitriﬁcation capacity of the UMSR, the pH of the
eﬄuent gradually increased and was close to that of the inﬂuent during
the later period of phase 3.
3.2. Diversity of the microbial community
To comprehend the eﬀects of the sludge acclimation method on the
performance of the UMSR, activated sludges S2 (60th day) and S3
(128th day) were sampled for DNA extraction and PCR ampliﬁcation
while the inoculated activated sludge (S1) was used as control. Reads
and diversity indices of microbial communities in the inoculum and the
acclimated sludges are illustrated in Table 1. Among the indices, Good’s
coverage of the three samples indicated that the sequence libraries
constructed in the present research could cover the diversity of mi-
crobial communities in the sludge samples (Zhen et al., 2014). Chao 1
and ACE species richness index indicated that maximum number of
species could be obtained when saturated sequencing was reached.
Shannon index was used to characterize the diversity of the microbial
community and it indicated results for species abundance and uni-
formity of species distribution.
As illustrated in Table 1, the Chao1, ACE, and Shannon indices for
sludges from phases 2 and 3 were remarkably higher than those of the
inoculum. The results indicate that species richness and diversity of
microbial communities had been remarkably enhanced. The change in
diversity was a response of the microbial community to adapt to en-
vironmental changes to better metabolize the pollutants. The more
complex microbial community structure of the UMSR suggests that the
ecological self-balancing capacity of the reactor gradually enhanced
with increasing acclimation time (Fig. 2). Compared with the inoculum
in which heterotrophic denitriﬁcation was the main metabolic process,
the diversity of acclimated microbial community increased because of
occurrence of simultaneous partial nitriﬁcation, anaerobic ammonium
oxidation and denitriﬁcation (SNAD) and carbon removal in the single-
stage UMSR. As illustrated in Fig. 2, the pollutant removal in phase 3
was signiﬁcantly better than that in the other phases.
3.3. Microbial community structure
Figs. 3 and 4 show the microbial community structure of the three
samples at phylum, class, and genus levels. The phylum level results
(Fig. 3a) demonstrate that the microbial community structure in phase
3 was obviously diﬀerent from that in the inoculum after acclimation.
The proportions of the main phyla Proteobacteria, Planctomycetes,
Bacteroidetes, Chloroﬂexi, and Acidobacteria were 45.31%, 1.11%,
31.07%, 4.08%, and 1.34% in S1, 37.55%, 9.02%, 8.15%, 14.63%, and
13.32% in S2, and 32.83%, 18.28%, 1.95%, 11.3%, and 10.92% in S3,
respectively (Fig. 3a). It is worth noting that these phyla are critical for
biological nitrogen removal during wastewater treatment. It was found
that the proportion of Planctomycetes in S3 increased signiﬁcantly from
1.11% to 18.28% in comparison to S1 due to long-term acclimation to
low DO and low C/N in the inﬂuent. This was because some species of
Planctomycetes displayed the ability to grow anaerobically and auto-
trophically via oxidation of ammonium (Fuerst, 2004). There was also a
marked increase in the proportions of Chloroﬂexi, Acidobacteria, and
Nitrospirae. Although the proportion of Proteobacteria decreased from
45.31% to 32.83%, it was still the highest in S3. Thus, Proteobacteria
still played a key role in the biodegradation process of the microaerobic
wastewater treatment system (Yang et al., 2014a). A previous study has
revealed that one of the most dominant aerobic ammonium oxidizing
bacteria (AerAOB) inoxygen-limiting process were Proteobacteria (Liu
et al., 2012a). Thus, the large proportion of Proteobacteria present in
the reactors contributed to the partial nitriﬁcation process. The α-
Proteobacteria, β-Proteobacteria, γ-Proteobacteria, or δ-Proteobacteria
were showed the highest proportions in each of the three sludge sam-
ples (Fig. 3b). In general, the α-proteobacteria carried out a wide
variety of metabolic reactions such as photosynthesis, nitrogen ﬁxation,
ammonia oxidation, and methylotrophy. In contrast to other studies on
the treatment of wastewater with low COD/TN ratio by the micro-
aerobic process, the proportion of Bacteroidetes decreased dramatically
from 31.07% to 1.95%.

UMSR, further analysis of the microbial communities at the genus level
was carried out (Fig. 4). The AOB (Nitrosospira) were only about 0.25%
in S1 because the inoculum was anoxic activated sludge obtained from
the AAO process. During the process of acclimation, the abundances
and diversity of ammonium oxidation-related bacteria gradually en-
hanced. The main species of AOB increased from just Nitrosospira to
Sphingomonas, Nitrosomonas, and Nitrosospira with respective propor-
tions of 0.93%, 0.35%, and 0.01% in the S3. This was diﬀerent from the
AAO process where Nitrosospira was the main species of AOB (Zhang
et al., 2017). In this study, the genera related to anaerobic ammonium
oxidizing bacteria (AnAOB) were detected as the predominant func-
tional microbes in S2 and S3 and the proportions of Candidatus Kue-
nenia, Candidatus Brocadia, Candidatus Scalindua and Candidatus Ana-
mmoxoglobus in S3 were 0.37%, 0.22%, 0.08%, and 0.03%, respectively
(Cabello et al., 2009). Compared to the proportion of AerAOB (1.29%),
the proportion of AnAOB was 0.70%, and the enrichment of these
genera contributed to excellent ammonium removal in the UMSR. This
was consistent with previous phylogenetic studies which indicate that
α- Proteobacteria and β-Proteobacteria related AerAOB and Plancto-
mycetales-like AnAOB were the predominant bacteria in the CANON
system (Liu et al., 2012b). AMX needed only ammonium, nitrite, and
CO2 as the major growth substrates and nutrients (Shively et al., 2009).
The structure of activated sludge granules and ﬂoc not only formed the
DO gradient but also produced a nutrient gradient. Camp et al., (2007)
found that the system of anammox was anoxic and characterized by
dynamic nutrient gradients.
Compared to S1, the diversity and proportion of AOB-related bac-
teria in the UMSR increased. In S1, the proportion of NOB (0.5%) was
greater than that of AOB (0.25%), while it was similar (1.32%) to that
of AOB (1.29%) after acclimation to low DO. The main mechanisms for
controlling NOB growth in the reactors were substrate gradient and
competition for oxygen by AOB and NOB (Brockmann and Morgenroth,

substrate limitations (Nowka et al., 2015).
During the start-up, a high proportion of NOB was enriched at the
end of phase 1 because of high DO. However, the autotrophic deni-
trifying bacteria and AMX were not enriched, resulting in NO3
−-N in
the eﬄuent reaching a concentration of 35 mg/L (Table 2). The low DO
ranging between 0.35 and 0.50 mg/L in phases 2 and 3 inhibited the
growth and activity of NOB. Although the DO in phase 3 was slightly
higher than that in phase 2, the DO concentration of 0.5 mg/L in phase
3 still could not meet the oxygen aﬃnity of NOB (Laanbroek and
Gerards, 1993). Therefore, the proportion of NOB for both phases (2–3)
gradually reduced from 1.60% to 1.32%. However, the saturation
constant of DO for AOB was as low as 0.2–0.4 mg/L (Laanbroek and
Gerards, 1993), therefore, the proportion of AOB increased from 0.25%
in the inoculum to 1.24% in phase 2, and 1.29% in phase 3. As a result,
the removal rate of ammonium gradually increased from 60% in phase
2 to 90% in phase 3. The increase in the proportion of AOB resulted in
the accumulation of nitrite which provided substrates for various sub-
sequent denitriﬁcation pathways. Heterotrophic denitriﬁcation was the
most important process for nitrogen removal in the inoculum because of
the proportion of heterotrophic denitriﬁers in the microbial community
(Fig. 4). After sludge acclimation, the proportion of heterotrophic de-
nitriﬁers decreased from 13.61% to 6.63%. In addition, the proportion
of heterotrophic denitrifying bacteria in the long-term low C/N ratio
inﬂuent was balanced, and the proportions in S2 and S3 were similar.
Under the condition of low C/N ratio in the wastewater, autotrophic
denitrifying bacteria which could denitrify with no supplement of
carbon source (Claus and Kutzner, 1985) were detected to increase
from 0% in the inoculum to 0.94% in phase 3, and the increase in the
proportion of autotrophic denitrifying bacteria played a key role in
denitriﬁcation in the UMSR resulting in a decrease of NO3
−-N in the
eﬄuent from 35 mg/L to 5 mg/L. As mentioned previously, anammox
was another nitrogen removal approach which needed no carbon
source (Chamchoi et al., 2008). The enrichment of autotrophic deni-
trifying bacteria contributed to excellent TN removal rate.
The long-term acclimation to low C/N ratio and low DO strength-
ened the role of AOB and autotrophic denitrifying bacteria while the
microaerobic conditions created a DO gradient in the activated sludge
granules and ﬂocs to allow aerobes, anaerobes, and facultative aerobes,
including AOB, NOB, AMX, autotrophic denitrifying bacteria, and het-
erotrophic bacteria, to thrive in diﬀerent depths of the granules and
ﬂocs. The various functional microorganisms could cooperate to re-
move pollutants in the UMSR, especially for nitrogen removal from
wastewater with a low COD/TN ratio, resulting in removal rates of 95%
for ammonia nitrogen and 90% for TN. The oxygen for the novel UMSR
was supplied by recirculating falling eﬄuent instead of aeration. The
supplied oxygen could meet the demands of nitrogen removal in the
reactor. Therefore, the energy consumption for treating wastewater
with low COD/TN ratio using this novel reactor will be signiﬁcantly
reduced. The economic feasibility will be further discussed in future
research.
3.4. Characteristics of sludge granules
Granular sludge was found to occur during the process of sludge
acclimation. The granulation process of microaerobic sludge included
three stages: seed sludge acclimation, ﬂocculation, and granulation.
The SEM images of granulation process were shown in E-supplementary
data and could be found in e-version of this paper online. After 30 days
of acclimation, irregularly shaped inoculum gathered regularly in
groups. A large volume of ﬁlamentous bacteria and extracellular poly-
meric substances (EPS) could be observed. The denitrifying sludge was
characterized by self-aggregation (Green et al., 1994) because deni-
trifying bacteria, such as heterotrophic bacteria, could produce high
quantities extracellular polysaccharides. Microaerobic granules were
aggregates of various minerals, inorganic compounds, EPS, and mi-
croorganisms (Adav and Lee, 2008). Additionally, EPS promoted ﬁne
particle debris to form granules. (Chen and Lee, 2015) claimed that
Brevundimonas, whose proportion in the UMSR sludge samples was
detected as 0.4%, is an eﬀective EPS producer. It has been reported that
Pseudomonas, Clostridium, Thauera, and Arthrobacter produce a large
number of viscous substances, such as excess alginate-like extracellular
polysaccharide and extracellular c-di-GMP, which are precursors of
granules (Yang et al., 2014b). These bacteria were detected in the
sludge samples. In an environment with low DO concentrations, the
ﬁlamentous bacteria could gain more DO and had growth advantages
because of increased speciﬁc surface area of their extended mycelium
which formed aggregate structures for sludge granules.
Supplementary data associated with this article can be found, in the
online version, at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biortech.2018.08.016.
Granulation of sludge occurred in the system within 50 days, how-
ever, the size of granules was small. After acclimation for 100 days,
larger and denser granules with an average diameter of 200 um were
observed. The formed granular sludge was regular and compact in ap-
pearance and gaps in the surface layer and the internal layer the
granular sludge existed for transporting internal and external sub-
stances. This was due to continuous production and release of gas from
the sludge granules by denitrifying bacteria and nammox bacteria
(Tang et al., 2011). The microaerobic system exhibited increased ni-
trogen removal as the size and structure of formed granules became
bigger and denser which is in agreement with the results of a previous
study (Huang et al., 2015).
In the internal structure of microaerobic granules, heterotrophs
used COD as a substrate to secrete excess EPS and autotrophic organ-
isms formed hydrophobic cell surfaces which formed dense anaerobic
cores and outer layers through the cluster-cluster aggregation me-
chanism (Cui et al., 2014; Tijani et al., 2015). There were abundant
microorganisms in the granules which were formed by polymerization
of a large number of spherical, bacillus, and ﬁlamentous bacteria, and
the bacilli were attached to the surface of granules or ﬂocs. AOB were
mostly rod-shaped, some heterotrophic bacteria were ﬁlamentous, and
AMX were mostly spherical. The varied microbial community structure
was the premise of rapid transformation and degradation of pollutants.
Moreover, the staggered lifestyle of the microbial community was
caused by nutrient transmission and strain reproduction which was
conducive to division of labour and cooperation among the microbial
community as well as eﬃcient removal of pollutants.
Rathnayake et al., (2015) also found granular processes for partial
nitriﬁcation and denitriﬁcation. Partial nitriﬁcation granules of AOB
dominated by Nitrosomonas were successfully cultured (Liang et al.,
2015). A partial nitriﬁcation aerobic granular reactor was used to treat

3.5. Integrating inferred niches and activities in a granule model
An ecological model proposed by (Speth et al., 2016) oﬀers an ex-
planation for the eﬀective performance of the SNAD reactor. Based on
the functions derived from the bacterial community structure at the
genus level, the ecological model, catalysed by the microbial biomass, is
suitable for the nitrogen cycle reactions of this study (Fig. 5). Because
the outer layer of the ﬂocculent biomass or granule surface is exposed
to oxygen, the main processes in the ﬂocculent biomass or granule
surface that are dominated by heterotrophic bacteria and nitriﬁers
(AOB and NOB) are aerobic oxidation of organic carbon to CO2 and
complete nitriﬁcation of ammonium to nitrate. The formed CO2 either
escapes to the atmosphere or is used by the primary producers (AOB
and NOB) for growth and biosynthesis. Inside the particles, a part of
nitrite is used by AMX to oxidize ammonium and produce nitrate. Based
on the stoichiometry of the anammox process, one mole of nitrite re-
duced produces 0.3 mol of nitrate resulting in accumulation of nitrate in
the eﬄuent (Fig. 2). Thus, excess nitrate accumulation in the system
might be mitigated by the presence of (partial) denitriﬁers that catalyse
the conversion of nitrate to nitrite.
A part of the formed nitrate can be reduced to nitrite using either
organic matter or hydrogen as the electron donor by heterotrophic and
autotrophic denitrifying bacteria, making additional nitrite available
for AMX. The hydrogen required for autotrophic nitrate reduction can
be formed through fermentation of organic matter by anaerobic fer-
mentation bacteria. The organic matter required for both nitrate re-
duction and fermentation can come from the inﬂuent, dead organic
matter in the granule, or extracellular granule matrix synthesized by
autotrophs. A part of the formed nitrite during autotrophic and het-
erotrophic denitriﬁcation converts to N2. AMX might metabolize the
NO to N2 (Kartal et al., 2010a,b).
4. Conclusions
To conduct municipal wastewater with low C/N ratio after anae-
robic digestion, a novel UMSR was constructed and its performance was
investigated at a temperature of 25 °C and an HRT of 24 h. Ammonium
and TN removal achieved in the UMSR were as high as 92.35% and
90.41%, respectively. Formation of particle sludge provided DO and
pollutant concentration gradients which were conducive to division of
labour and cooperation among microbial communities as well as eﬃ-
cient removal of pollutants. The inferred niches and activities of the
microbial communities in the granule model oﬀered an explanation for
the eﬀective performance of the UMSR.
